name: Esther Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing history and politics. I live at home in Wexcombe with my mum, who's a nurse on nights, and my little brother Tomas, who's twelve. I get the bus to the university and I work Friday and Saturday nights at the Regent cinema, selling tickets and sweeping popcorn. The rest of the week is seminars, reading and making Tomas his tea when Mum is on shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does university feel so far?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Bigger and lonelier than I thought. I enjoy the seminars, especially one on the French Revolution, but I'm commuting so I miss the evening social side. I use an AI tool sometimes to summarise a reading, then I read the real thing anyway. Money is tight, though Mum tops up my phone bill when she can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. AI is useful for small things, but people overestimate it. I'd tell my friends not to build their lives around predictions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be uneasy, because Mum's nights are our main income and I'm the one who covers when she's ill. My shifts help with rent. If the cinema closes screens, I lose that. That's a real worry on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep the cinema shifts, study, and look at the teaching or civil service route after my degree. I'd also put aside ten pounds a month for emergencies, though it's hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried about money, but not frightened. It's a normal kind of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the pressures on your family even if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Regent has been struggling since streaming. The manager, Colin, says they might close one screen. That would take away half my shifts. That's more likely to hurt me than anything in a lab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra hours if the cinema offered them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Colin early. I'd ask the university for a hardship fund application form, and I'd look at the library for any weekday evening work.

I'd say AI is useful for small things but people **overestimate** it.

do: Keep the cinema shifts and the **seminars**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit different jobs differently. I'd say we should wait for evidence rather than guess. In seminars I'd bring it up and ask what history students can do that machines can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious about the civil service route. It's mostly writing, checking and answering letters, exactly what the tools take. Teaching feels safer, because kids need a person in the room. But it's a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both options open. I'd try the tools to see what they can do, and use my history degree to work on research skills that are harder to automate. I'd also talk to a teacher I trust, Mr Haines, who writes my references.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a quiet way. It's like being told the weather will change without knowing when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the jobs you want, teaching or civil service, hold up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the graduate job data the careers service publishes, and ask people two years ahead of me. If trainee posts shrink, I'd shift my plan toward a teaching qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check whether the degree is still worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to keep at the reading and the thinking. Whatever happens, knowing how to argue and check a source stays useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and we need serious public help. I'd say it quietly to my friends and loudly to my MP. Two years is too short to build new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd have a degree and no job to use it. Mum's job might survive for a while, because nursing is hands-on, but I don't trust that. The thing I fear is that we'd need my income and I'd have none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at university until I knew more, because leaving costs me the place. I'd get more hours at the Regent or somewhere else, and I'd ask Mum if we can combine money for the rent. I'd also look at nursing or a hands-on route, since that's the work robots reach last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, really. My head says we'd cope and my stomach says we wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas is twelve. If I'm out of work and Mum's on shift, who looks after him? That would be the hardest thing. I'd have to put my plans on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would tell me to stay in school and not worry. But she'd be the one worrying. I'd tell her we should plan together.

fieldNote: Her fear is about **household** income and her brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a plan, if you start soon. I'd tell people to learn something useful, and I'd tell the government to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel steadier. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years to get a first job. By 2031 I'd have a bit of work history. It's tight but possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, apply for a teaching qualification, and work at the Regent until then. I'd save whatever I can and teach myself the tools so I'm not behind. I'd also help Tomas choose subjects that suit a changing world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not panicked. I'd be able to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a shock. Five years is a countdown, but one I can plan around. I'd use it to get a qualification that needs a real person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do once it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it arrives, I'd try to be in a classroom or a hospital, where people matter. And I'd be there for Mum when she retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to adapt, and that's not nothing. I'd tell friends to enjoy their studies and keep an eye on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel mostly fine. By twenty-eight I could be teaching, maybe renting my own flat. The change would come, but slowly enough that I could ride it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, qualify as a teacher, and save steadily. I'd learn the tools as they become normal in schools. I'd also help Mum with her pension planning, because she's careful but alone with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only in the background. There's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Tomas to be through school and happy. I'd want Mum to be able to cut her night shifts. That's the main thing I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be true by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job I like, a stable flat, and some money behind me. Nothing grand. I think that's possible with ten years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my household would have no space to adapt. What would help is real hardship money for students whose families depend on them, and clear information from the university about what jobs will actually exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that students with caring jobs at home don't always say it. My brother is part of my plan, and nobody asks about that. Please do.

headlineQuote: Students with caring jobs at home don't always say it. My brother is part of my plan, and nobody asks about that.
portrait: Esther is an eighteen-year-old **history and politics** student who sells cinema tickets two nights a week.
She lives with her night-shift nurse mother and twelve-year-old brother, and helps look after him.
Centre in her politics and steady about change, she waits for evidence before acting.
She sees civil service work as exposed and teaching or nursing as safer routes.
Her mood climbs to **anxious** in the two-year case, because the household has no spare capacity.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because her household would have no room to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: **Hardship money** for students whose families depend on them.
Clear **university information** about which jobs will exist.
